<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:existence}
Let $G=\langle a,b\rangle$ be a finite group, where $a,b$ are distinct nonidentity elements. If $\langle ba^{-1}\rangle$ is normal in $G$, then $\operatorname{Cay}(G;\{a,b\})$ has two arc-disjoint directed Hamiltonian paths.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:extension}
Assume $g\ge2$. The complementary choices specified by $E$ extend to two arc-disjoint Hamiltonian paths with both terminal vertices in $H$ if and only if
\[
 u_E\notin\mathcal F(q,B).
\]
There are at most four exceptional residues for even $q$ and at most six for odd $q$.

If $g\ge3$, choose any two distinct indices $i,j\in\{1,\ldots,g-1\}$ and prescribe the choices on all other nonterminal cosets. If $E_0$ denotes those prescribed to use $b$ in the first color, then one of
\[
 E_0,\qquad E_0\cup\{i\},\qquad E_0\cup\{i,j\}
\]
extends. A single free nonterminal coset does not suffice for this guarantee.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:spectra}
Let $q\ge3$ and $A,C\in\mathbb Z_q\setminus\{0,-1\}$. If $q$ is even, then
\[
 \operatorname{dist}(Z_q(A),Z_q(C))=
 \begin{cases}
 0,&A\equiv C\pmod2,\\
 1,&A\not\equiv C\pmod2.
 \end{cases}
\]
If $q$ is odd and neither coefficient is $c=(q-1)/2$, then the spectra intersect. For the central coefficient,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:central-distance}
 \operatorname{dist}(Z_q(c),Z_q(D))
 =\min\{\gcd(q,D),\gcd(q,D+1)\}-1.
\end{equation}
For every $D\in\mathbb Z_q$, the degenerate distances are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:degenerate-distance}
 \operatorname{dist}(Z_q(0),Z_q(D))=\gcd(q,D+1)-1,\qquad
 \operatorname{dist}(Z_q(-1),Z_q(D))=\gcd(q,D)-1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:forcing}
Let $P$ be a Hamiltonian path in $\operatorname{Cay}(G;\{a,b\})$, and write $\eta=ba^{-1}$. Every left coset $xH$ not containing the terminal vertex uses one generator throughout. If the terminal vertex is $\tau$, the choices at
\[
 \tau\eta,\tau\eta^2,\ldots,\tau\eta^{q-1}
\]
are a string of $a$-choices followed by a string of $b$-choices, with either string possibly empty.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
The arcs $x\to xb$ and $x\eta\to x\eta a=xb$ have the same head. Hence a $b$-choice at $x$ prevents an $a$-choice at $x\eta$. On a coset with all outgoing arcs present, a single $b$-choice propagates around the entire $\eta$-orbit. On the terminal coset, deleting its unique terminal position leaves the asserted ordered string.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:terminal-cosets}
If two arc-disjoint Hamiltonian paths have their terminal vertices in distinct left cosets of $H$, their two unused arcs can be added to give a decomposition into two Hamiltonian cycles. In particular, the existence of a pair implies the existence of a pair whose terminal vertices lie in the same left coset of $H$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
On the terminal coset of the first path, the second path makes a complete constant generator choice. The first path therefore uses the opposite generator at every position except its terminal vertex. Add the opposite generator's arc there, and perform the analogous operation for the other path. Both colors now make complementary constant choices on every coset. Each is a permutation: the two possible predecessors of any head lie in the same $\eta$-orbit, and precisely one is chosen. The arc added to each spanning path closes that path into a Hamiltonian cycle. Deleting both cycles' outgoing arcs at a common vertex gives the last assertion.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:realization}
If $s\in Z_q(A)$ and $v\in Z_q(C)$ satisfy $|s-v|\le1$, the prescribed nonterminal choices extend to two arc-disjoint Hamiltonian paths with terminal vertices in $H$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Color $0$ omits the outgoing arc at $0$, uses $a$ at $1\le z<s$, and uses $b$ at $s\le z<q$. For color $1$ use the table below, omitting the outgoing arc at $h$ and using $a$ at all remaining coordinates outside the indicated interval.
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{@{}ccc@{}}
\toprule
Relation & Terminal coordinate $h$ & Coordinates using $b$ in color $1$\\
\midrule
$v=s$ & $s\pmod q$ & $1,\ldots,s-1$\\
$v=s+1$ & $s$ & $0,\ldots,s-1$\\
$v=s-1$ & $s-1$ & $1,\ldots,s-2$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
Empty intervals are interpreted as empty sets. At every coordinate where both colors have an outgoing arc, their generators differ.

The first map in~\eqref{eq:return-map} is $R_{A,s}$. Under the reflection $x=h-z$, the second map becomes
\[
 x\longmapsto x+C+1-\chi_1(h-x),
\]
which is $R_{C,v}$ in each row. Thus each partial return joins all $q$ segments into one path. Exactly one vertex of $Ha$ has no incoming terminal arc in each color; it is the initial vertex of that path. Each resulting path visits every vertex of $G$, and their arc sets are disjoint.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:fixed-reduction}
For a fixed set $E$ of nonterminal coset choices, an extension with both terminal vertices in $H$ exists if and only if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:fixed-reduction}
 \operatorname{dist}(Z_q(u_E),Z_q(u_E-B))\le1.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Sufficiency is Lemma~\ref{lem:realization}. For necessity, left-translate by the inverse of the first terminal vertex, an element of $H$. This preserves $E$ and places that terminal at $0$. Arc forcing gives a unique cut $s$ for color $0$.

Let $h$ be the second terminal coordinate. At every $z\ne0,h$, the second color uses the opposite generator. When $1<s<q$, its choices at $s-1,s$ would be $b,a$, causing an incoming conflict. Thus $h\in\{s-1,s\}$. The choice at zero is free. After reflection about $h$, the four possibilities $(h,\chi_1(0),v)$ are
\[
 (s-1,0,s-1),\quad(s-1,1,s),\quad
 (s,0,s),\quad(s,1,s+1).
\]
The reflected coefficient is always $C=u_E-B$.

When $s=1$, the other color either uses $a$ at every nonterminal position, giving $v=1$, or uses $b$ only at zero and has terminal coordinate one, giving $v=2$. When $s=q$, the symmetric possibilities give $v=q$ or $q-1$. The constant-choice cases allow arbitrary terminal coordinates, with the same reflected cut. This includes $q=2$ and completes the classification.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:endpoints}
For $q\ge2$ and $D\in\mathbb Z_q$, write $d_0=\gcd(q,D)$ and $d_1=\gcd(q,D+1)$. Then
\begin{align}
 \min Z_q(D)&=d_1,&\max Z_q(D)&=q+1-d_0,\label{eq:endpoints}\\
 Z_q(-D-1)&=q+1-Z_q(D),&
 s&\equiv d_1\pmod2\quad(s\in Z_q(D)).\label{eq:parity}
\end{align}
In particular, $Z_q(0)=\{1\}$ and $Z_q(-1)=\{q\}$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The translation $T_{D+1}$ has $d_1$ cycles. If $s<d_1$, the support of $\tau_s$ misses at least one cycle. At $s=d_1$ it meets each cycle once, and its cyclic rejoining makes one cycle. This proves the minimum. Reflection by $z\mapsto-z$ conjugates $R_{D,s}$ to $R_{-D-1,q+1-s}$, proving the reflection identity and the maximum. Finally,
\[
 \operatorname{sgn}(Q_{D,s})=(-1)^{q-d_1+s-1},
\]
which equals the sign $(-1)^{q-1}$ of a $q$-cycle exactly when the stated parity condition holds.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:profile}
Define
\[
 z_0=L,\qquad z_i=L+2\sum_{j=1}^iH_j\quad(1\le i\le k).
\]
Then $z_k=N-R$, and, with $x=s-1$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:profile}
 j_D(s):=\operatorname{cyc}(Q_{D,s})-1=
 \begin{cases}
 L-x,&0\le x\le L,\\
 \min\{x-z_{i-1},z_i-x\},&z_{i-1}\le x\le z_i,\\
 x-(N-R),&N-R\le x\le N.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
In an internal excursion, every closed component of $R_{D,s}$ has primitive displacement $U_i$ and length $\mathcal L(U_i)$. Moreover,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:profile-zeros}
 Z_q(D)-1=\{z_0,\ldots,z_k\},\qquad
 j_D(s)=\operatorname{dist}(s,Z_q(D)).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:sector}
For two distinct rays of positive multiplicities $p,t$, the intervening multiplicity $M$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:sector-exact}
 M\ge\Theta(p,t)
 =\frac{(p-1)(t-1)+\gcd(p,t)-1}{2}
 \ge\frac{(p-1)(t-1)}2.
\end{equation}
The assertion includes either or both boundary rays when their multiplicities are positive.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Let $U,V$ be the primitive vectors. Their lengths are at most $N/p,N/t$. Every positive pair $i,j$ with $i/p+j/t\le1$ supplies a distinct lattice point $iU+jV$ strictly between the rays and of length at most $N$. The intervening multiplicity counts all these points, including distinct multiples on the same primitive ray. The number of such pairs is $\Theta(p,t)$: pairing the interior points of $[0,p]\times[0,t]$ across its center leaves $\gcd(p,t)-1$ points on the diagonal $i/p+j/t=1$ and gives the formula.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:length}
Every internal weight $H$ of $Z_q(D)-1$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:length}
 (L+R+2)H\le N.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
For $(x,y)\in\Lambda_D$ with $x,y>0$, reducing the defining congruence modulo $d_1$ and $d_0$ gives $d_1\mid x$ and $d_0\mid y$. Hence
\[
 \mathcal L(x,y)\ge d_0+d_1=L+R+2.
\]
Now use $H\mathcal L(U)\le N$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:sector-filled}
Let $S=\{s_0<\cdots<s_k\}\subseteq\{0,\ldots,N\}$, with $k\ge1$, and suppose its gaps have positive integer half-lengths $h_i=(s_i-s_{i-1})/2$. Its boundary weights are $L=s_0$ and $R=N-s_k$; its ordered weights are
\[
 L,h_1,\ldots,h_k,R.
\]
We call $S$ \emph{sector-filled} if any two distinct positions carrying positive weights $p,t$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:weak-sector}
 M\ge\frac{(p-1)(t-1)}2,
\end{equation}
where $M$ is the sum of the intervening weights. We say that it satisfies the length inequality if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-length}
 (L+R+2)h_i\le N\qquad(1\le i\le k).
\end{equation}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:five-runs}
The ordered union of two separated sector-filled sequences has at most four runs.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Suppose that five consecutive runs have labels
\[
 S_0,\quad T_0,\quad S_1,\quad T_1,\quad S_2.
\]
The $S$-gaps containing $T_0,T_1$ have respective half-lengths $\alpha,\gamma$. The $T$-gap containing $S_1$ has half-length $\beta$. Reversing the order if necessary, which interchanges $T_0$ and $T_1$, assume $\alpha\le\gamma$.

Let $M$ be the multiplicity between the $\alpha$- and $\gamma$-gaps of $S$. The first and last points of $S_1$ span length $2M$. The two ends of the $\beta$-gap lie at least $\delta$ outside those points. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:beta-lower}
 \beta\ge M+\delta
 \ge\frac{(\alpha-1)(\gamma-1)}2+\delta
 \ge\frac{(\alpha-1)^2}2+\delta.
\end{equation}

In the $T$-sequence, let $p$ be the weight immediately preceding the run $T_0$: it is its preceding gap weight, or the left boundary weight if $T_0$ is the first $T$-run. In the former case that gap contains $S_0$, so $p\ge\delta$. In the latter case $\min T\ge\delta$, again giving $p\ge\delta$. The multiplicity between $p$ and the $\beta$-gap is half the span of $T_0$, at most $\alpha-\delta$. Thus
\[
 \frac{\beta-1}{2}
 \le\frac{(p-1)(\beta-1)}2
 \le\alpha-\delta,
\]
so $\beta\le2\alpha-2\delta+1$. Combining this with~\eqref{eq:beta-lower} yields
\[
 (\alpha-3)^2+6\delta-10\le0.
\]
Its left side is at least two, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:four-runs}
Two separated sector-filled sequences satisfying the length inequality cannot have exactly four runs.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Restrict to the convex hull of $S\cup T$ as above and rename its length $N$. Exchange $S,T$ if necessary so the runs are $S_0,T_0,S_1,T_1$. Then
\[
 \min S=0,\quad \max S=N-r,\qquad
 \min T=\ell,\quad \max T=N,
\]
where $\ell,r\ge\delta\ge2$. Let $[x,y]$ be the $S$-gap containing $T_0$, of half-length $\alpha$, and $[z,w]$ the $T$-gap containing $S_1$, of half-length $\beta$. Both half-lengths are at least $\delta$.

At the three transitions between runs, separation gives
\[
 x\le\ell-\delta,\qquad y-z\ge\delta,\qquad N-w\le r-\delta.
\]
Since $y=x+2\alpha$ and $w=z+2\beta$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:four-upper}
 N=x+2\alpha+2\beta-(y-z)+(N-w)
 \le\ell+r+2\alpha+2\beta-3\delta.
\end{equation}
On the other hand, the two length inequalities imply
\begin{align*}
 2N&\ge(r+2)\alpha+(\ell+2)\beta\\
   &=4(\alpha+\beta)+(r-2)\alpha+(\ell-2)\beta\\
   &\ge4(\alpha+\beta)+2(\ell+r)-8.
\end{align*}
Twice~\eqref{eq:four-upper} contradicts this, because $6\delta-8>0$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:confinement}
Let $S,T\subseteq\{0,\ldots,N\}$ be sector-filled sequences satisfying the length inequality. Suppose their convex hulls overlap. If $\delta=\operatorname{dist}(S,T)\ge2$, then, after exchanging the sequences if necessary, all of $T$ lies in one gap of $S$. More precisely, for two consecutive points $x,x+2H$ of $S$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:confinement}
 x+\delta\le\min T\le\max T\le x+2H-\delta.
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Overlapping hulls and separation give at least three runs. Lemma~\ref{lem:five-runs} gives at most four, and Lemma~\ref{lem:four-runs} excludes four. With three runs, the middle run is the whole of one sequence and is enclosed by consecutive points of the other. Separation gives~\eqref{eq:confinement}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:length-needed}
The two hypotheses rule out different configurations. Sector filling alone forces a separated nested sequence into one gap. The length inequality excludes interlacing. For example, at $N=10$ the sequences
\[
 S=\{0,6,8\},\qquad T=\{2,4,10\}
\]
satisfy even the exact sector bound~\eqref{eq:sector-exact}, but have distance two and four alternating runs. Their largest weight is three and their boundary sum is two, so $(L+R+2)h=12>N$. Thus the length inequality distinguishes this abstract interlacing from a cut spectrum.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Assume first that $A,C$ are nondegenerate and that their spectral distance is $\delta\ge2$. Their endpoint divisors are proper divisors of $q$, so the convex hulls of $Z_q(A)-1$ and $Z_q(C)-1$ overlap. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:confinement}; exchange $A,C$ so that the latter spectrum is contained in one gap of the former. Put
\[
 a=\gcd(q,A),\quad b=\gcd(q,A+1),\qquad
 c_0=\gcd(q,C),\quad d=\gcd(q,C+1).
\]
Comparing endpoints gives $c_0-a\ge\delta$ and $d-b\ge\delta$, hence $c_0,d\ge3$. Since $\gcd(c_0,d)=1$ and $c_0d\mid q$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:divisor-sum}
 c_0+d\le\frac{c_0d}{3}+3\le\frac q3+3;
\end{equation}
this is $(c_0-3)(d-3)\ge0$.

Let $H$ be the height of the containing gap. Its width is at least
\[
 2H\ge q+1-c_0-d+2\delta\ge\frac{2q}{3}+2.
\]
Since $H=\lfloor(q-1)/\mathcal L(U)\rfloor$, the corresponding positive primitive vector has length less than three. It is therefore $(1,1)$, and its lattice congruence gives $2A+1=0\pmod q$. Consequently $q$ is odd and $A=(q-1)/2$.

For this coefficient the two steps are opposite units. A simple path in the resulting bidirected cycle cannot change direction, because that would revisit the preceding vertex. Hence $Z_q((q-1)/2)=\{1,q\}$. Lemma~\ref{lem:endpoints} gives~\eqref{eq:central-distance}. In every other nondegenerate case the distance is at most one, and~\eqref{eq:parity} gives the exact parity statement. Finally, the two degenerate spectra in Lemma~\ref{lem:endpoints} give~\eqref{eq:degenerate-distance}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:failure}
For every $q\ge2$ and $B\in\mathbb Z_q$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:failure-identity}
 \mathcal F(q,B)=\{u\in\mathbb Z_q:\operatorname{dist}(Z_q(u),Z_q(u-B))>1\},
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal F(q,B)$ is given by~\eqref{eq:Fminus}--\eqref{eq:Fcentral}.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The cases $u=0$ or $u-B=-1$ give~\eqref{eq:Fminus}; $u=-1$ or $u-B=0$ give~\eqref{eq:Fplus}, by the degenerate distance formulas. The only other possibilities are $u=c$ or $u-B=c$ for odd $q$. Multiplying the other coefficient and its successor by the unit two in~\eqref{eq:central-distance} gives the two conditions in~\eqref{eq:Fcentral}. They also handle any coincident entries of the displayed pairs. For $q=2$, the two singleton cut spectra are always at distance at most one.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:three}
For all $q\ge2$, $B,u\in\mathbb Z_q$, at least one of $u,u+1,u+2$ lies outside $\mathcal F(q,B)$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
For $q\le6$ the assertion follows directly from~\eqref{eq:Fminus}--\eqref{eq:Fcentral}. For instance, the nonempty sets at $q=6$ are $\{0\}$, $\{2,5\}$, $\{0,3\}$, and $\{5\}$.

For even $q\ge8$, the set is contained in the two consecutive pairs $\{-1,0\}$ and $\{B-1,B\}$. A triple of consecutive residues in this union forces $B\in\{\pm1,\pm2\}$. Substituting these values in the two gcd conditions leaves at most two exceptional residues.

Now let $q\ge7$ be odd and write $h=2^{-1}$ in $\mathbb Z_q$. The candidate set is
\[
 \{-1,-h,0\}+\{0,B\}.
\]
After multiplication by two, it becomes $I\cup(I+2B)$ with $I=\{-2,-1,0\}$. A three-term progression of step two in this union has two terms in one of the two translates of $I$. Their difference cannot be four when $q\ge7$; they must be adjacent terms of the progression and the endpoints of that translate. Placing the remaining term in the other translate forces
\[
 B\in\{\pm1,\pm2,\pm3/2\}.
\]
For $B=\pm1$ the exceptional set has one point. For $B=3/2$ it is contained in $\{-1,B\}$, and for $B=-3/2$ in $\{0,B-1\}$. If $B=2$, the pair~\eqref{eq:Fminus} is absent. Neither $0$ nor $1$ can occur from the other two pairs when $q\ge7$. Thus neither endpoint pair $\{-1,0\}$ or $\{1,2\}$ required above is present. The case $B=-2$ follows by the reflection $u\mapsto-u-1$, which sends $\mathcal F(q,B)$ to $\mathcal F(q,-B)$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:B-units}
Suppose $w,z$ are units modulo $q$ with $wB=zB=B$. Then for every $u$, at least one of
\begin{equation}\label{eq:three-states}
 u,\qquad u+w,\qquad u+w+z
\end{equation}
lies outside $\mathcal F(q,B)$.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Let
\[
 q_0=\prod_{p^e\parallel q,\ p\nmid B}p^e.
\]
Every common divisor of $q$ with $B-1,B+1,2B-1$, or $2B+1$ divides $q_0$. Thus each exceptional residue modulo $q$ projects to an exceptional residue modulo $q_0$, by Proposition~\ref{prop:failure}. In the odd case the central residue projects to $(q_0-1)/2$. If $q_0\le2$, the original exceptional set is empty.

Otherwise $B$ is a unit modulo $q_0$, so $w\equiv z\equiv1\pmod{q_0}$. If all three residues in~\eqref{eq:three-states} were exceptional, their images would be three consecutive exceptional residues modulo $q_0$, contradicting Lemma~\ref{lem:three}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The exact criterion is Proposition~\ref{prop:fixed-reduction} together with Proposition~\ref{prop:failure}. For the two free cosets, let
\[
 u_0=t+\sum_{k\in E_0}r^k.
\]
The relations~\eqref{eq:intro-coordinates} give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:B-invariant}
 (r-1)B=0\pmod q.
\end{equation}
Hence $r^i$ and $r^j$ are units fixing $B$. The three prescribed extensions have return residues
\[
 u_0,\qquad u_0+r^i,\qquad u_0+r^i+r^j.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:B-units} supplies a successful residue, and Lemma~\ref{lem:realization} completes its paths.

For sharpness, take the consistent parameters
\[
 (q,g,r,t)=(12,9,1,4)
\]
and prescribe $a$ in the first color on every nonterminal coset except one. Here $B=5$, and the two possible residues are $4,5$, both in $\mathcal F(12,5)$. Proposition~\ref{prop:fixed-reduction} excludes every terminal completion of these choices. With two free cosets the three possible residues are $4,5,6$; the last succeeds with cuts $(1,2)$. This proves the stated optimality.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
When $g\ge3$, apply Theorem~\ref{thm:extension}, prescribing $a$ on all other nonterminal cosets.

When $g=2$, choose $E=\varnothing$. The two return coefficients are $A=t$ and $C=-t-r-1$. The relations $r^2=1$ and $rt=t$ imply
\[
 r(t+1)=t+r.
\]
Thus $c=\gcd(q,t+1)=\gcd(q,t+r)$ is an initial successful cut for both coefficients by Lemma~\ref{lem:endpoints}. Lemma~\ref{lem:realization} applies with $(s,v)=(c,c)$, including $q=2$.

When $g=1$, the group is cyclic and $a=\eta^t$, $b=\eta^{t+1}$. The generators being nonidentity means $t\notin\{0,-1\}$, so $q\ge3$. Theorem~\ref{thm:spectra} applies to $t,-t-1$. If one is the odd central coefficient, both are, and they share the endpoint cuts. Otherwise the theorem supplies equal or adjacent cuts. Use the terminal table of Lemma~\ref{lem:realization} directly on this single copy of $\mathbb Z_q$. Its two partial maps are the required paths.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:metacyclic}
Every finite nonabelian metacyclic group admits a generating pair $a,b$ of distinct nonidentity elements for which $\operatorname{Cay}(G;\{a,b\})$ has two arc-disjoint Hamiltonian paths.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Choose a cyclic normal subgroup $K=\langle\eta\rangle$ with cyclic quotient, and let $aK$ generate $G/K$. Put $b=\eta a$. Then $G=\langle a,b\rangle$ and $\langle ba^{-1}\rangle=K$. Noncommutativity ensures $1<K<G$, so $a,b$ are distinct and lie outside $K$. Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:existence}.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:cut-move}
For $0\le d<N$, the values $j(d+1),j(d)$ differ by one. If both are positive, the two graphs have the same primitive cycle class.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Put $v=d-D$ and $w=v+1$. The move from $P_d$ to $P_{d+1}$ deletes $w\to d+1$ and inserts $v\to d+1$. If $w$ is on the open path, this splits off one cycle. If it is on a closed cycle, that cycle joins the open path. All other cycles remain. When both counts are positive, at least one unchanged cycle is present in both graphs, and its class determines the class in each.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:local-crossing}
If $1\le d<N$ and $j(d-1)=j(d)+1=j(d+1)$, then $j(d)=0$. The primitive classes $U_-,U_+$ of the two neighboring graphs satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:det}
 \det(U_-,U_+)=q.
\end{equation}
In particular, the slope increases at such a minimum.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Let $v=d-D$. The cycle removed from $P_{d-1}$ contains the horizontal edge $v\to d$; call it $\Gamma_-$. The cycle added in $P_{d+1}$ contains the vertical edge $v\to d+1$; call it $\Gamma_+$.

Translate the embedded graph $P_{d+1}$ by $\epsilon(e_1-e_2)$ with $0<\epsilon<1$. An original horizontal edge meets a translated vertical edge precisely when their original tails coincide. In~\eqref{eq:Pd}, the first graph's horizontal condition is $i>d-1$, and the second graph's vertical condition is $i<d+1$. Their common index is exactly $i=d$; Figure~\ref{fig:local-crossing} shows the corresponding local lifts.

The other possible crossing is an original vertical edge and a translated horizontal edge with the same original head. Their indices are $i,i+1$ modulo $q$. The required inequalities $i<d-1$ and $i+1>d+1$ are incompatible. The wrap at $q-1$ adds no case, since $i<d-1\le q-3$. Parallel translated edges are disjoint. Thus the graphs have exactly one transverse intersection, at the two specified edges, of positive sign.

It follows that $\Gamma_-$ and the translate of $\Gamma_+$ have intersection number one, giving~\eqref{eq:det}. If $P_d$ contained a closed component, it would remain in both neighbors, forcing its primitive class to be parallel to both $U_-$ and $U_+$. This contradicts~\eqref{eq:det}.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:residue-count}
The number of points $(x,y)\in\Lambda_D$ with $x,y>0$ and $x+y\le N$ is $(q+1-d_0-d_1)/2$. Equivalently,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:total-multiplicity}
 N=H_x+H_y+2\sum_U H(U).
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
For each length $1\le l<q$, the unique possible second coordinate is
\[
 y_l\equiv-Dl\pmod q,\qquad0\le y_l<q.
\]
An internal point occurs precisely when $0<y_l<l$. There are $d_0-1$ lengths with $y_l=0$ and $d_1-1$ with $y_l=l$, and the two classes are disjoint. On the other lengths, $l\mapsto q-l$ sends $y_l$ to $q-y_l$ and exchanges $y_l<l$ with $y_l>l$. Thus exactly half of the remaining $q+1-d_0-d_1$ lengths contribute an internal point. Grouping the points by their primitive rays gives~\eqref{eq:total-multiplicity}.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
At $d=0$, all edges are horizontal except for the missing terminal edge, so $j(0)=H_x$. Similarly $j(N)=H_y$. There is a zero of $j$: either an endpoint is already zero, or the positive endpoint counts have horizontal and vertical classes, and Lemma~\ref{lem:cut-move} prevents a positive sequence of counts from carrying both classes.

On a positive excursion the primitive class $U$ is constant. The open component contains at least one vertex, so $j(d)\mathcal L(U)\le N$ and $j(d)\le H(U)$. Lemma~\ref{lem:local-crossing} excludes every positive local minimum. Since the counts change by one, an internal excursion rises to one peak and then descends. At each intervening zero the primitive slope strictly increases. Hence each primitive ray is visited at most once. The initial horizontal excursion decreases from its already maximal height $H_x$ to zero, and the final vertical excursion increases from zero to $H_y$.

Let $h(U)$ be the heights of the internal excursions actually visited. Their total duration gives
\[
 N=H_x+H_y+2\sum_{U\text{ visited}}h(U).
\]
Each $h(U)\le H(U)$, while~\eqref{eq:total-multiplicity} gives the same identity using every internal primitive ray at full height. Thus every ray occurs and every height is attained. Reversing $d=q-s=N-(s-1)$ gives~\eqref{eq:profile}. Its zeros and unit slopes give~\eqref{eq:profile-zeros}; the common primitive class gives the assertion on cycle lengths.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
